courses.title: Islamic Media Literacy
courses.subtitle: Navigate the digital world with confidence, discernment and Islamic values.
outcomes: Explain what media is and the key elements every message contains
Recognize the main types of contemporary media and how they influence you
Evaluate the credibility of a news story or website in minutes
Apply Qur'anic principles of verification to what you read, watch and share
courses.description:
Media shapes how the world sees Muslims — and how we see ourselves. This course gives you the tools to understand how media works, question what you consume, and choose content that brings you closer to Allah rather than further away.

It is built for teens, parents, educators and anyone who wants to become a thoughtful, responsible media consumer and creator.

lessons.title: What Is Media?
lessons.summary: Why media matters for every Muslim today
lessons.body:
## Media is everywhere

Every day you are surrounded by media: the videos in your feed, the news on TV, the billboards on the highway, the podcasts in the car. **Media** is any channel used to carry a message from a sender to an audience.

Media doesn't just inform us — it shapes what we believe is normal, important, beautiful and true. That is why understanding it is not optional for a Muslim today.

## Why media literacy matters for Muslims

- **Representation:** Mainstream coverage of Muslims is often shaped by stereotypes. If we can't read media critically, we may start to believe those portrayals — even about ourselves.
- **Identity:** Young Muslims spend hours each day online. What they watch forms their role models, values and sense of belonging.
- **Responsibility:** Every "share" is an action we are accountable for. Spreading something false, even unknowingly, has consequences.

> Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate and create media — with understanding and intention.

## A simple mindset shift

Instead of asking *"What is this telling me?"*, start asking:

1. **Who** made this, and why?
2. **What** is left out?
3. **How** is it trying to make me feel?
4. **Is it beneficial** for my dunya and akhirah?

## Reflection

Think about the last three pieces of media you consumed today. Who created them, and what did they want from you — your attention, your money, your opinion?

lessons.title: The Key Elements of Media
lessons.summary: Sender, message, medium, audience and purpose
lessons.body:
## Every message has a structure

Whether it's a 15-second reel or a feature film, every piece of media is built from the same key elements. Learning to spot them is the first step to thinking critically.

| Element | Question to ask | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Sender** | Who created this? | A news network, a brand, an influencer |
| **Message** | What idea is being communicated? | "This product will make you happy" |
| **Medium** | What channel carries it? | TikTok, newspaper, radio, YouTube |
| **Audience** | Who is it aimed at? | Teens, parents, voters |
| **Purpose** | Why was it made? | To inform, persuade, entertain or sell |
| **Effect** | What does it change? | Your mood, opinion or behavior |

## Techniques to watch for

- **Framing** — what's inside the frame (and what is cut out) changes the story.
- **Music and sound** — the same image feels heroic or threatening depending on the soundtrack.
- **Word choice** — "freedom fighter" vs. "militant," "protest" vs. "riot."
- **Repetition** — a message repeated often enough starts to feel true.

## Try it

Pick one advertisement or news clip. Fill in all six elements from the table above. What did you notice that you missed the first time?

lessons.title: Types of Contemporary Media
lessons.body:
## The media landscape today

Media has evolved quickly — from printed pages to algorithms that know what you'll watch next.

### Traditional media
**Newspapers, magazines, radio and television.** Content is produced by professional organizations with editors. It reaches large audiences, but a small number of owners often control what gets covered.

### Digital media
**News websites, streaming services, podcasts and online video.** Anyone can publish, which opens doors for new voices — including ours — but also makes quality and accuracy uneven.

### Social media
**Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, Facebook, Snapchat.** Content is created by users and ranked by algorithms designed to maximize attention. Emotional, extreme or shocking content tends to spread fastest.

### Journalism
The professional practice of gathering, verifying and reporting news. Good journalism follows ethics: accuracy, fairness, and accountability. It can exist on any of the platforms above.

## What this means for you

- Know **which kind of media** you're looking at — the rules and incentives are different.
- Remember that **algorithms are not neutral**. They show you what keeps you scrolling, not what is true or good for you.
- Digital and social media are also **an opportunity**: Muslims can now tell our own stories directly to millions.

> The same tools that spread misinformation can spread beneficial knowledge. The difference is the intention and integrity of the person using them.

lessons.title: Spotting Fake News
lessons.summary: A practical checklist for judging credibility

quiz.question: What is the first thing you should check about an unfamiliar news website?
options: How many likes the post has
Who runs the site and whether they are accountable
Whether the headline makes you angry

quiz.question: A shocking claim appears on only one website. What is the best next step?
options: Share it quickly so others are warned
Look for the same report from other independent, reputable sources
Assume it is true because it is detailed

lessons.body:
## Why fake news spreads

Websites and posts can look professional while spreading falsehoods. False stories often spread faster than true ones because they are designed to trigger strong emotions — fear, anger or outrage.

## The 6-step credibility check

1. **Check the source.** Who runs the site? Is there an "About" page, real names and contact details?
2. **Read beyond the headline.** Headlines are written to get clicks. Does the article actually support the claim?
3. **Check the author.** Are they real? Do they have expertise or a track record?
4. **Look for evidence.** Are there links to original documents, data or named sources?
5. **Check the date.** Old stories are often recirculated as if they were new.
6. **Cross-check.** Is the same story reported by other independent, reputable outlets?

## Red flags 🚩

- ALL CAPS, excessive exclamation marks, or "they don't want you to know this!"
- URLs that imitate real outlets (e.g. extra letters or unusual endings)
- Images with no source — try a reverse image search
- Pressure to "share before it's deleted"

## Practice

Find a viral claim in your feed this week. Run it through the six steps. Did it hold up?

lessons.title: Media Through an Islamic Lens

quiz.question: Surah Al-Hujurat (49:6) instructs believers who receive news from an unreliable source to…
options: Verify it before acting on it

lessons.body:
## Verification is an Islamic value

Long before "fact-checking" was a profession, the Qur'an set a clear standard. In Surah Al-Hujurat (49:6), believers are told that when an untrustworthy person brings them news, they must **verify it**, lest they harm people out of ignorance and then regret what they have done.

This single principle is the heart of Islamic media literacy: **pause, verify, then act.**

## Three principles to carry with you

### 1. Truthfulness (sidq)
The Prophet ﷺ warned that it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything they hear. Sharing without checking is not neutral.

### 2. Intention (niyyah)
Ask yourself *why* you are consuming or sharing something. Is it to learn, to help, to remember Allah — or simply to pass time and feed outrage?

### 3. Benefit (manfa'ah)
Entertainment that is consumed and forgotten leaves nothing behind. Seek out — and create — content that benefits you and others in this life and the next.

## A personal media audit

For one week, note what you watch and how you feel afterward. Then decide:

- **Keep:** content that teaches, inspires or brings you closer to Allah
- **Limit:** content that wastes time without harm
- **Remove:** content that misleads, degrades or pulls you away from your values

> In Allah we must put our trust — and with the tools He has given us, we can choose media that reflects the truth.

courses.title: Storytelling & Filmmaking Foundations
courses.subtitle: Learn to tell authentic Muslim stories — starting with the phone in your pocket.
outcomes: Find and shape a story with a clear message
Plan a short video with a simple shot list
Film clean, steady, well-lit footage on a phone
Edit a rough cut that holds an audience's attention
courses.description:
Our stories deserve to be told by us. In this hands-on course you will learn how to find a story worth telling, plan it, film it with simple equipment and shape it in the edit.

By the end you will have a plan for your own short film or video — and the confidence to make it.

lessons.title: Why Our Stories Matter
lessons.body:
## Who tells our story?

For decades, stories about Muslims have mostly been told by people outside our communities — and too often they have relied on stereotypes. When we don't tell our own stories, others will tell them for us.

## Stories shape identity

Young people learn who they can become through the characters they see on screen. When the only Muslim characters are villains or victims, that leaves a gap. Authentic stories fill it with **dignity, depth and possibility**.

## Our tradition is a storytelling tradition

The Qur'an itself teaches through stories — of prophets, nations and ordinary people facing extraordinary tests. Allah calls these accounts *ahsan al-qasas*, the best of stories, and they carry lessons for those who reflect.

## Your mission in this course

By the end of these lessons you'll plan and shoot a short video (1–3 minutes) that tells a true, meaningful story from your community.

> Start small. A powerful two-minute story about your grandmother can move more hearts than a big-budget film with nothing to say.

lessons.title: Finding Your Story
lessons.body:
## The three ingredients

Every compelling story — from a documentary to a 60-second reel — needs:

1. **A character** we care about
2. **A challenge** they face
3. **A change** — what they learn, overcome or become

## Where to find stories

- A family member's migration journey
- A local masjid volunteer who quietly feeds hundreds every week
- A young Muslim pursuing an unusual dream
- A moment of history from our heritage, retold for today

## Write your logline

A logline is one sentence that captures your story:

> *When [character] faces [challenge], they must [action] in order to [goal].*

**Example:** *When a retired teacher in Virginia loses her sight, she must learn to recite the Qur'an by ear in order to keep teaching her grandchildren.*

## Exercise

Write three loglines for three different stories. Share them with a friend and ask which one they'd most want to watch — and why.

lessons.title: Filming With Your Phone
lessons.body:
## Your phone is a film camera

Modern phones shoot beautiful video. What makes footage look professional is not the camera — it's **stability, light and sound**.

## Stability
- Use a tripod, or brace your elbows against your body.
- Move slowly. Hold every shot for at least **5–10 seconds**.
- Shoot horizontally (16:9) for YouTube and the web; vertically (9:16) for reels and shorts.

## Light
- Face your subject toward a window — soft daylight is the most flattering light there is.
- Avoid putting a bright window **behind** your subject.
- Lock exposure and focus (tap and hold on most phones).

## Sound
Audiences forgive average video, but not bad audio.
- Get the microphone close: a $20 clip-on mic makes a huge difference.
- Record in quiet rooms with soft furnishings (carpets, curtains).
- Record 30 seconds of "room tone" — silence — to help in editing.

## The shot list
For every scene, capture:
- **Wide** — where are we?
- **Medium** — who is here?
- **Close-up** — what do they feel?
- **Details** — hands, objects, textures (great for editing)

lessons.title: Editing Basics
lessons.body:
## Editing is where the story is written again

You've filmed your scenes — now you shape them into a story.

## Free & simple tools
- **CapCut** or **iMovie** — great for beginners
- **DaVinci Resolve** — free, professional-grade

## A simple workflow
1. **Organize:** put all clips in one folder and name them clearly.
2. **Assembly cut:** place your best moments in story order. Don't worry about polish.
3. **Rough cut:** trim every clip. If a moment doesn't serve the story, cut it.
4. **Fine cut:** add B-roll (detail shots) over interviews, adjust pacing.
5. **Sound & color:** balance audio levels, add subtle music, correct color.
6. **Titles & export:** add your title, captions and credits.

## Golden rules
- **Start strong.** You have about three seconds to earn attention.
- **Cut on action.** Transitions feel smooth when cut in the middle of a movement.
- **Add captions.** Most social video is watched on mute.
- **Choose music with care** — and only use music you have rights to (or consider nasheeds and voice-only soundtracks).

## Your assignment
Edit a 1–3 minute short from your logline. Send it to us — we'd love to feature student work!

courses.title: Heroes of Our Heritage
courses.subtitle: Meet the Muslim scholars and inventors who shaped our world.
outcomes: Tell the story of three pioneering Muslim scientists
Connect their discoveries to technology we use every day
Draw lessons on curiosity, patience and excellence (ihsan)
courses.description: Our youth deserve role models drawn from our own rich civilization. Each lesson in this series tells the story of a Muslim pioneer — who they were, what they discovered, and what their example teaches us today.

lessons.title: Ibn al-Haytham: Father of Optics
lessons.summary: The scientist who explained how we see
lessons.body:
## Who was he?

Abu Ali al-Hasan **Ibn al-Haytham** was born around 965 CE in Basra, Iraq, and did much of his greatest work in Cairo. In the West he became known as *Alhazen*.

## What did he discover?

For centuries, many people believed that our eyes send out rays to "touch" what we see. Ibn al-Haytham showed through careful experiments that **light travels from objects into the eye**.

His *Book of Optics* (Kitab al-Manazir) explained reflection, refraction and how lenses work — and it influenced European scientists for hundreds of years.

## The first "camera"

He studied the **camera obscura** — a dark room with a tiny hole that projects an image of the outside world onto the wall. This is the basic principle behind every camera, including the one in your phone. Every film we make today owes something to his work!

## The scientific method

Ibn al-Haytham insisted that ideas must be **tested by experiment**, not just accepted because a famous person said them. He wrote that a seeker of truth should be critical even of the books he reads — and of himself.

## Lesson for us

Curiosity is a form of worship when it leads us to reflect on Allah's creation. Like Ibn al-Haytham, question carefully, test patiently, and let the evidence speak.

lessons.title: Mariam al-Asturlabi: Master of the Astrolabe
lessons.body:
## A 10th-century innovator

**Mariam al-Asturlabi** (also known as Al-'Ijliyah) lived in the 10th century in Aleppo, Syria. Her title, *al-Asturlabi*, comes from the instrument she mastered: the **astrolabe**.

## What is an astrolabe?

An astrolabe is a handheld model of the sky. With it, people could:

- tell the time by the sun or stars
- find their latitude and direction
- determine the direction of the **qiblah** and prayer times
- support navigation across deserts and seas

## Her contribution

Mariam learned the craft from her father and became so skilled that she was employed in the court of the ruler Sayf al-Dawla. Her intricate, precise designs advanced the accuracy of these instruments — part of the long chain of knowledge that leads to today's navigation tools.

In 1990, a main-belt asteroid — **7060 Al-'Ijliya** — was named in her honor.

## Lesson for us

Mariam's story reminds us that Muslim women have always been scholars, makers and innovators. Excellence (*ihsan*) in our craft — whatever it is — is part of our tradition.

lessons.title: Al-Khwarizmi: The Birth of Algebra
lessons.body:
## The scholar of the House of Wisdom

**Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi** (c. 780–850 CE) worked at the famous **House of Wisdom** in Baghdad, a center of learning where scholars translated, debated and advanced knowledge from across the world.

## The birth of algebra

His book *Al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala* gave the world a systematic way to solve equations. The word **"algebra"** comes from *al-jabr* in its title.

He wrote it to help people solve real problems — inheritance shares, trade, land measurement — showing that mathematics could serve the community.

## From his name: "algorithm"

When his works were translated into Latin, his name became *Algoritmi*. Today the word **algorithm** describes the step-by-step instructions that power computers, apps and the social media feeds we studied in our Media Literacy course!

## Lesson for us

Knowledge in Islam is meant to benefit people. Al-Khwarizmi turned complex problems into clear steps anyone could follow. What problem in your community could you help solve with your talents?
